data: © NASA / Viking Project — Chryse Planitia landing site, NASA Planetary Data System.

First fully successful Mars surface mission. Viking 1 operated for over six years on the surface — the longest-duration surface mission until Opportunity (a rover) broke the record in 2010. It returned the first colour images from the Martian surface, conducted the first life-detection experiments (results famously inconclusive), and characterised the regolith and weather.
First long-duration in-situ Martian science — every modern lander runs on Viking's playbook.

Viking 1 touched down in Chryse Planitia on July 20, 1976 — the first successful US lander on Mars, exactly seven years after Apollo 11. Its 2,245-sol surface mission (6.3 years) included the first colour images from Mars, the first in-situ biology experiments (with ambiguous results), and a daily weather record. Final transmission November 1982 after a command upload accidentally overwrote the antenna-pointing parameters.
